newsitem.title: FRANCE: French minister slams dairy firms in milk row. [CORRECTED 22:14 GMT]
newsitem.headline: French minister slams dairy firms in milk row. [CORRECTED 22:14 GMT]

text.p: France's farm minister hit out at the dairy industry on Wednesday after talks failed to end a row which has brought farmers into country lanes to protest against falling milk prices.
Philippe Vasseur emerged from four hours of talks between dairy farmers, distributors and milk processors saying the processors had blocked a deal to freeze prices.
"I am profoundly disappointed," Vasseur told reporters after hosting the talks at the farm ministry.
Dairy farmers had blocked deliveries to hypermarkets in various parts of France on Tuesday to draw public attention to a gradual slide in milk prices they say threatens their jobs.
The protesters set up roadblocks before dawn and turned back delivery trucks, accusing big distribution firms of orchestrating the fall in prices.
No new date was set for talks to ease the dispute, which also sees the milk distributors and processors at odds with each other over who is to blame for the increasingly bitter dispute.
Vassseur attacked what he called the "intransigence" of industrial milk companies which he said had blocked "any possible opening" towards a compromise.

"It is a short-sighted position which does not bode well ahead of new discussions about the Common Agricultural Policy," he said in an apparent threat to look more favourably on the farmers' position in future European Union farm negotiations.
The EU's 30-year-old CAP regime is up for discussion this autumn amid calls by the EU's executive Commission for price reductions under an existing regime of production quotas.

Before then, processors want farmers to accept a drop of two percent in the price they receive for milk, currently 1.9 to 2.0 francs a litre. They say the cut is needed to help make up for an eight-percent drop in prices further down the delivery chain.

A spokesman for the processing firms, Xavier Paul-Renard of the FNIL dairy industry association, refused to accept blame for the failure of Wednesday's (corrects from Thursday's) talks and said price cuts were necessary to fend off competition from Europe and elsewhere.

Farmers' spokesman Jean-Michel Lematayeur said he was "deeply disappointed" and promised that the producers would remain determined to highlight their case, though without saying whether any further protests were planned.
Tuesday's unexpected protest alarmed the farm ministry and drew wide publicity in the week leading up to the first round of parliamentary elections on May 25. A runoff round is set for June 1.

About four percent of the French workforce is directly employed in agriculture. But although the electoral system gives these voters greater weight at the voting booths, pollsters say traditionally prickly farm issues will have little sway in this election, which has been dominated mainly by economic austerity.
